problem: R2R reference paths are all direct-to-goal shortest paths, and the dominant metrics (SR, NE, SPL) only look at goal completion. As a result, an agent can score well while ignoring the described route, so current VLN evaluation cannot measure instruction fidelity. SED (Touchdown) does compare paths, but it is binary per action, has no soft penalties, and is zero unless the agent succeeds.
motivation: Following the path described matters in practice: a robot that reaches the goal by another route may cross unwanted or dangerous areas. Prior evidence also shows language matters less than it should on R2R. Low-fidelity speaker-augmented instructions still help, and agents do surprisingly well without language, which suggests the metrics are insensitive to fidelity. Many R2R paths end where others begin, so longer and twistier paths with human instructions can be built for free.
key_idea: The paper proposes CLS (Coverage weighted by Length Score), a soft path-fidelity metric, and R4R, built by concatenating R2R paths into longer non-shortest paths. Using CLS as an RL reward yields agents that follow the instructed route and rely more on language.
insight:
On R2R, goal-oriented and fidelity-oriented rewards give nearly the same results (val-unseen SR 41.1 vs 40.8), because on shortest-path references a goal reward already implies path conformity. Keeping only the last 5 instruction tokens recovers much of the gap between no instructions and full instructions, which shows that R2R mostly tests where to stop. On R4R the gap opens:
- The fidelity agent raises val-unseen CLS from 20.4 to 34.6 and lowers NE from 8.45 to 8.08 m.
- Its SPL drops (10.2 vs 7.7), showing SPL is misleading when the reference path is not direct-to-goal.
- The language ablation is the telling one. The goal-oriented agent's CLS is unchanged with only the last 5 tokens (20.4 → 20.4), while the fidelity agent drops from 34.6 to 25.3. So a fidelity reward is what forces the agent to use the instruction.
method: R4R dataset construction: join R2R paths A and B when d(a_|A|, b_1) < d_th, inserting the shortest connecting path C. Every instruction combination is paired, giving N_A·N_B instructions per extended path. Result: 233,613 train / 1,035 val-seen / 45,162 val-unseen samples; mean reference length ~20 m vs ~10 m shortest-to-goal.

Metric desiderata: five properties are proposed: (1) path similarity, (2) soft graph-distance penalties, (3) unique optimum, (4) scale invariance, (5) tractability. PL, NE, ONE, SR, OSR, SPL and SED are analysed against them; SPL violates (1) and (3), and SED violates (2).
CLS metric: PC = mean over reference nodes r of exp(-d(r,P)/d_th). EPL = PC·PL(R). LS = EPL/(EPL+|EPL−PL(P)|). CLS = PC·LS. It is computable in O(|P||R|) after all-pairs Dijkstra.

Agent: reimplemented RCM reasoning navigator (without intrinsic reward).
  - Instruction encoding: GloVe embeddings, fine-tuned, fed to a BiRNN encoder.
  - Visual input: 36-view panoramic CNN features plus sin/cos orientation, pooled by attention.
  - State and actions: an LSTM tracks agent state; a bilinear action predictor scores navigable directions (panoramic action space) using text and visual attention contexts.

Training: behavior cloning warm-start, then REINFORCE with an advantage baseline. Each policy-gradient batch is interleaved with K behavior-cloning batches, with K decaying exponentially toward pure policy gradient.

Rewards: the goal-oriented reward is dense (per-step reduction in distance to goal plus a terminal success indicator). The fidelity-oriented reward is sparse and terminal: 1[success] + CLS(trajectory, R). A CLS-shaping term gave no noticeable difference.
Language ablations at evaluation: last 5 tokens only, no instruction, or an arbitrary validation instruction (the arbitrary case behaved like no instruction).

numbers_note: The tables' PL (agent path length) column is mapped to TL. The 'no instructions' ablation rows are not listed individually; e.g., on R4R val-unseen CLS is 23.0 (fidelity) vs 17.4 (goal). The arbitrary-instruction ablation is only described in text as similar to no instructions, with no numbers. Speaker-Follower and Random rows are the authors' own runs, but they are baselines and are excluded. The authors note their goal-oriented RCM matches published RCM on val-unseen but is lower on val-seen.
results: On R4R val-unseen, the CLS-rewarded (fidelity-oriented) RCM reaches CLS 34.6 and NE 8.08 m. The goal-oriented RCM gets CLS 20.4 / NE 8.45 m, and the reimplemented Speaker-Follower gets CLS 29.6. The fidelity agent's SR (26.1 vs 28.6) and SPL (7.7 vs 10.2) are lower, which the authors take as evidence that SPL is misleading for non-shortest paths. On R2R both reward types perform similarly (val-unseen SR 40.8 vs 41.1; CLS 50.9 vs 47.4; SPL 35.1 vs 32.7). The fidelity agent's R4R CLS drops from 34.6 to 25.3 with only the last 5 tokens, while the goal agent's stays at 20.4, showing that only the fidelity agent actually uses the instruction.
limitations: R4R instructions are two independently written R2R instructions concatenated, and the connecting segment C between the paths is not described by any instruction, so parts of the reference path are unannotated.

Absolute performance on R4R is low (best val-unseen CLS 34.6, NE 8.08 m). Only one agent family (a reimplemented RCM, weaker than published on val-seen) is studied, and the fidelity reward trades off some SR/SPL.

CLS's unique-optimum guarantee assumes an acyclic reference path and a shared start node. A random walker gets a non-trivial CLS (29.0 on R2R val-unseen, 22.3 on R4R val-unseen, above the goal-oriented RCM's 20.4), so CLS has a relatively high floor.
